newsitem.title: UK: British sheep cloning advances genetic technology.
newsitem.headline: British sheep cloning advances genetic technology.

text.p: The cloning of a sheep using the cell of an adult sheep takes genetic science a huge step forward, making it much easier to produce genetically engineered animals, researchers said on Monday.
Ian Wilmut of the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh, working with biotechnology company PPL Therapeutics, cloned the sheep using an embryo cell and the cell from another sheep's mammary gland.
The same group cloned sheep using two embryonic cells last year, but they said using adult cells made the procedure more efficient.

Wilmut's team removed the nucleus, which contains the genetic material, from the embryo cell. They then took a cell from another sheep's mammary gland inside its udder and fused it to the emptied cell.
"The nucleus goes into the empty egg," said Dr Ron James, Managing Director of PPL, which has filed a patent for the process. "It behaves as if it has gone right back to the start."

All cells contain the genes to create a whole animal or plant, but normally a skin cell divides to make another skin cell, a muscle cell another muscle cell and so on. Roslin's fusion process makes the emptied cell with the new nucleus act like an embryo, and it starts growing an animal from scratch.

PPL now uses technology developed at Roslin to genetically engineer animals that produce human proteins in their milk. Their main product is AAT, a sheep's milk now in clinical trials for use in treating cystic fibrosis.
They have been using the old technology, which introduces genes into an early embryo. This process only works in about five percent of cases -- the rest come out as just plain sheep.
That means 100 sheep are born for every five that produce useful transgenic chemicals.
James said with the new technology, one of the five percent of transgenic animals can be cloned to create a whole herd of sheep that produce the protein.
"We can select them out and grow lots of them, all in the lab and then and only then do we make the animals and every one of them has got the genetic modification that we want," he said.

That means fewer animals are used in the process and the material needed can be produced more quickly. "It opens the way to making products that are more difficult to do using present technology. We can remove genes as well as add genes."

Companies that produce genetically engineered pigs for possible use in human organ transplants could also benefit from the technology, James said. The pigs now are manipulated to produce human proteins as part of their organs, so that the immune systems of the human recipients do not reject them.
The procedure still is not highly effective, Wilmut acknowledges. During the experiment they created hundreds of clones, some of them using embryos and some using the adult mammary cells.
More than 60 percent of the foetuses created using the process died during pregnancy.
"Eight ewes gave birth to live lambs," they wrote in their report in Nature. One weak lamb died a few minutes after birth, although Wilmut's group was unable to find any defect or disease.
Only one lamb was born from the mammary cell group.
